context: linear network · large pipes & box culverts, outfall first, finished before the road surface

brief.intro: New to this project type? A stormwater network takes rain off roads and plots and carries it to a safe discharge — a wadi, a canal, the sea, a detention pond or a soakaway. It looks like a sewer network but the pipes are much bigger (often box culverts), the flows arrive in sudden peaks, and the system starts at road gullies that can only be finished with the kerb and asphalt. Like sewers it works by gravity and is built from the outfall upstream. Two things drive the programme: the heavy civil work of large pipes and culverts, and the season — an open, unfinished drain in the rainy season floods the site, so the main lines and the outfall should be working before the rains.

glossary.plain: the area whose rain runs to one drain.
the point where the network discharges to a watercourse, pond or the sea.
a rectangular concrete conduit used where a round pipe would be too large.
the grated inlet at the kerb that collects road water.
the concrete wall at the end of a pipe or culvert that retains the embankment.
a basin that stores the storm peak and lets it out slowly.

the size of storm the network is designed to carry, e.g. a 1-in-10-year storm.

must_get_right: Build the outfall and the trunk drain first and work upstream, so every finished length can actually drain.
Aim to have the trunk lines and outfall working before the rainy season; show the season in the calendar and check which open excavations it catches.
Gullies and their connections can only be completed with kerbs and before the final asphalt layer — tie them to the road programme, not to the drain crew.
Box culverts are structures, not pipe laying: formwork, reinforcement, concrete and curing (or precast delivery and cranes) need their own durations.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities are organised by drain line (outfall, trunk, laterals) and by road, in construction order from the outfall upstream, with the gullies tied to the road-works programme.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Standard site calendar, with the rainy season marked: excavation and concrete in low areas are planned outside it where possible, and reduced productivity is assumed inside it.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: Outfall → trunk drain / culvert upstream → laterals → manholes, each length excavate → structure / pipe → cure → backfill. Gullies are linked to kerbs and to the last asphalt layer. Ponds and the pumping station run in parallel and must be ready before the network is declared operational.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: The discharge point is approved; the road-works contractor follows the drain crew in the agreed order; groundwater is as in the soil report; precast units are delivered to the planned call-off.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: The schedule tracks the following as milestones because they drive the programme:

rows: Precast box-culvert units & large concrete / GRP pipe

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Large pipes and culverts need wide trenches, cranes and road closures. The outfall may be in a watercourse or at the shoreline with its own environmental and tidal limits.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Main risks: rain flooding open works, late precast or pump delivery, clashes with existing utilities at the large trench width, and gullies finished out of sequence with the road. Contingency is held before the rainy season date and before road surfacing.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 by drain line and road; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the excavation, culvert and gully crews — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
